section.name: Deployment Applicability
section.t: The repair overhead this mechanism adds is justified only where the delivery path actually loses packets, and multicast loss characteristics differ by orders of magnitude across access technologies. FEC strength (P and Interleave Depth) is a per-path deployment choice, expressed by which tracks each endpoint carries, not a protocol constant.

li.t: Engineered low-loss segments. On managed PON or DOCSIS delivered over a provisioned VLAN, steady-state loss is typically far below 10^-6. Disabling FEC for such a path is signaled by omitting the repair track from the tracks that path's endpoints carry. Adding repair symbols on such a path spends bandwidth to recover losses that do not occur.

FEC-capable broadcast PHYs. ATSC 3.0, DVB-S2/S2X, and 5G broadcast already apply bit-error correction on their own radio link (e.g., LDPC/BCH in ATSC 3.0 and DVB-S2/S2X). Application-layer FEC is NOT a duplicate of that correction: it recovers packet erasures the PHY cannot address -- bursts when reception falls below the PHY threshold (rain fade, mobility, indoor reception), and losses on upstream aggregation or backbone hops that the last-hop PHY never sees. Its value on these paths comes primarily from Interleave Depth spreading a burst across the time domain, not from the code rate. On a one-way broadcast downlink with no return path, application-layer FEC is the only available erasure-recovery mechanism -- which is why ATSC 3.0 (see Section 12) specifies it above the PHY.
Public Internet and AMT tunnels. Loss is real and bursty; a non-trivial repair count with interleaving is RECOMMENDED.

section.name: Interaction with Multicast QUIC
section.t: defines a one-way QUIC transport in which a multicast channel carries QUIC packets bearing STREAM or DATAGRAM frames, recovering loss via unicast repair (the MC_CHANNEL_ACK mechanism) and defining no Forward Error Correction of its own. This FEC scheme MAY be used as the recovery layer on such a channel, and is RECOMMENDED over unicast repair for broadcast-scale audiences, where per-receiver retransmission does not scale.
When this scheme is carried over a multicast QUIC channel:

li.t: Symbol-to-datagram mapping. Each source or repair symbol (one MMTP packet, per ) SHOULD be carried in exactly one QUIC DATAGRAM frame. This aligns the erasure unit (a lost QUIC packet) with the FEC symbol, so one lost packet erases exactly one source symbol. STREAM framing SHOULD NOT be used for FEC-protected media on a multicast channel: a lost packet then spans a byte range crossing symbol boundaries, defeating symbol-aligned recovery.

Crypto boundary. FEC encoding operates on application-layer objects, ABOVE the QUIC packet protection of . Unlike bare multicast UDP -- which lacks QUIC's integrity guarantees (see Section 14.4) -- the multicast QUIC binding applies a shared-key AEAD per packet. A sender computes source and repair symbols over the unencrypted objects; the channel then applies its AEAD; a receiver decrypts each surviving packet and recovers erased objects from the decrypted source and repair symbols. A lost packet cannot be decrypted, but its object is reconstructed from other verified symbols, so recovery does not depend on possessing it.

Integrity of recovered objects. The integrity frames of authenticate the bytes of each delivered packet. A FEC-reconstructed object was never carried in a single packet and is therefore NOT individually covered by a packet hash; it inherits trust transitively from the verified surviving symbols used to reconstruct it. Deployments requiring per-object authentication of recovered data SHOULD additionally apply an object-level scheme (for example the manifest-based bc-provenance profile of Section 7.2) computed below the FEC layer, which survives reconstruction.

Repair channel versus unicast repair. A publisher using this scheme broadcasts repair symbols on the multicast channel (the repair track) rather than relying on unicast retransmission. Receivers covered by the repair flow SHOULD NOT drive unicast repair for losses the FEC recovers, preserving the O(1) sender cost that motivates broadcast FEC. Unicast repair MAY be retained as a last resort for losses exceeding the repair budget. Section 11.4 specifies that last resort.

section.t: Symbols delivered over a multicast QUIC channel are deduplicated by their Source Block Number and Encoding Symbol ID; normatively requires only this deduplication, and Section 8.3 permits combining them with symbols received from other paths.

section.name: Receiver Repair Policy
section.t: This section specifies what a receiver of a multicast or AMT leg does with a base-instance block of a source track that in-band FEC has not recovered by the block's FEC deadline (Section 9). A receiver on a reliable MoQ/QUIC leg relies on transport retransmission (Section 3) and does not need it, and nothing in this section adds a deadline or a timer to such a leg.

Every block receives in-band FEC processing. A receiver MUST attempt to recover every block, whatever its class, from the source and repair symbols received on its multicast and AMT paths, together with any it receives on other paths (Section 8.3), up to the block's FEC deadline. The rest of this section governs only a block that is still unrecovered at that deadline: the receiver does not hold all of its authored source symbols (K, or SSB_length for a short source block, Section 7.4), and decoding from the symbols it holds has not recovered them.

The policy distinguishes keyframe-bearing blocks, whose loss can stop video decoding until the next Random Access Point (RAP), from other blocks, whose loss damages only frames up to the next RAP. Keyframe-bearing blocks are protected by priority unicast repair and are the only blocks whose loss may stall video. Other blocks are repaired on a best-effort basis and, when repair fails, concealed. Every frame and audio sample a receiver presents MUST be presented at its authored time on the presentation clock shared by its tracks, and a receiver MUST NOT stall video or pause that clock except for a keyframe-bearing block (Section 11.4.2).

section.name: Block Classification
section.t: A base block of a video source track is keyframe-bearing if it carries, or may carry, any part of a RAP: a fragment of a RAP MFU, or of the FT=0 or FT=1 data unit that governs it ( Sections 4.3 and 5.1). The receiver classifies each block when the block reaches its FEC deadline, from two inputs and only from them: in-band evidence in the source packets it holds, and the catalog-authored timing of the track, that is its group structure, one MPU per group of the catalog group duration ( Sections 4.3 and 4.4.2), and its keyframe interval ( Section 4.4.3). K and the block's SSB_length, once known (Section 7.4), fix which SS_IDs belong to the block, and interleaveDepthMs with reorderToleranceMs fixes the deadline at which the class is taken (Section 9).

The receiver first bounds what the block's missing source symbols can carry. The lower bounding packet is the last source packet it holds, in SS_ID order, before the block's first missing source symbol; the upper bounding packet is the first source packet it holds after the block's last missing source symbol. Either may lie in an adjacent block. Only FEC source symbols count: the AL-FEC signaling object of Section 8 carries no SS_ID and is never a bounding packet. A publisher MUST assign the base SS_IDs of a track's source packets in increasing order along the authored order of Section 4.3, so every data unit the missing symbols can carry lies between the data units of the two bounding packets, those two included.
The block is keyframe-bearing if any of the following holds:

li.t: A source packet the receiver holds from the block sets RAP_flag, carries two Source FEC Payload IDs (Section 8.5.1), or is an FT=0 packet, or two source packets it holds from the block carry different MPU sequence numbers.

The two bounding packets carry different MPU sequence numbers, or the lower bounding packet is the FT=0 packet or the first FT=1 packet of its MPU, or belongs to the first FT=2 sample of its MPU. The missing symbols can then carry part of a group-start RAP, or of the metadata that governs it ( Section 4.3).

The catalog carries a usable keyframe interval, and the closed interval between the authored decode times ( Section 5.1) of the samples of the two bounding packets contains an instant a positive whole number of keyframe intervals after the decode time of the first sample of their MPU. Where a bounding packet is an FT=1 packet, its time is the decode time of the first sample it describes. The interval is keyframeIntervalTicks, or keyframeIntervalMs converted to the track timescale where that conversion is exact; an inexact keyframeIntervalMs gives no usable interval.

section.t: The block is non-keyframe-bearing only when none of these holds, the catalog carries a usable keyframe interval, the receiver holds both bounding packets, and it can determine every value item 3 needs. Every other block is of unknown class, and a receiver MUST treat a block of unknown class as keyframe-bearing. In particular:

li.t: A block for which the receiver holds no lower or no upper bounding packet at its FEC deadline is of unknown class, as is one for which it cannot determine a decode time that item 3 needs.

On a video track whose catalog entry carries no usable keyframe interval, the receiver cannot exclude a keyframe after the group start from any span, so every block of the track is keyframe-bearing or of unknown class.

Where every block spans at least one whole group, as in the model of Sections 8.1 and 8.2, every block contains a group start and is keyframe-bearing. The non-keyframe class arises only where the source symbols of one group span several blocks, as on an mmtp-packaged track whose blocks the span bound of interleaveDepthMs (Section 5.1) closes before the group ends (Section 7.4).

section.t: A receiver MUST NOT classify a block from any input other than those this section names; in particular, the absence of RAP_flag on the packets it holds says nothing about a packet that was lost. A publisher that wants receivers to be able to apply the non-keyframe treatment of Section 11.4.3 publishes an exact keyframe interval, which then binds every keyframe of the track ( Section 4.4.3).

The blocks of a track that the catalog identifies as audio are treated by Section 11.4.4, not classified by this section. A track that the receiver cannot identify from its catalog entry is treated as video.

section.name: Keyframe-Bearing Blocks
section.t: When a keyframe-bearing block is still unrecovered at its FEC deadline, a receiver that holds a MoQ session with a relay serving the block's repair track MUST request on-demand unicast repair for it, with the priority of Section 11.4.5. The request is a standalone FETCH , over QUIC, of the repair-track group numbered with the block's SBN (Sections 6.3.2 and 6.3.5): on layer 0, and on further layers in layer order where the receiver needs more symbols than layer 0 carries. The FETCH MAY be limited to the object range that covers the block's shortfall. The repair symbols it returns are deduplicated against the symbols already held by SBN and ESI (Section 8.3) and fed to the same decoder; their SSB_length also conveys a short block's authored length (Section 7.4). The receiver MUST NOT delay this request behind any non-keyframe or audio repair; Section 11.4.6 covers its interplay with a keyframe overlay. A FETCH completes or fails by MoQ Transport events, its last object or an error; a receiver MUST NOT declare it failed on a locally chosen timeout.

Only a keyframe-bearing block may stall video. While its unicast repair is outstanding, the receiver MAY hold video presentation for it. The block is unrecoverable when its unicast repair fails or completes without recovering it, or when the receiver holds no MoQ session through which to request it (for example a receiver that consumes an MMTP stream without a MoQ session, Section 1.1). If the data of an unrecoverable block that the receiver could not recover includes, or may include, any part of a RAP (Section 11.4.1), the receiver treats the track as discontinuous, MAY stall video, and does not resume video before the next RAP ( Section 6.1, step 6). Otherwise, as when it holds or has recovered every part of the block's RAPs (including through a keyframe overlay, Section 11.4.6), it conceals the block's remaining loss as for a non-keyframe block (Section 11.4.3).
If the next RAP arrives complete before a keyframe repair completes, the repair is moot: the receiver resumes from that RAP and SHOULD cancel the FETCH.

section.name: Other Video Blocks
section.t: For a non-keyframe-bearing block of a video track, in-band FEC remains the primary repair. A receiver MAY also request unicast repair for it, in the form of Section 11.4.2, but only on the terms of Section 11.4.5: never ahead of or concurrently with keyframe repair, and only within the budget that keyframe repair leaves unspent.

When such a block is unrecovered -- at its FEC deadline without unicast repair, or when its unicast repair has not completed by the presentation time of the first media it would repair -- the receiver MUST NOT stall. It conceals the affected frames, and every frame that depends on them, until the next RAP, and keeps presentation and audio/video synchronization running:

li.t: Concealment fills the presentation interval of the frames it replaces and ends at the authored presentation time of the next frame the receiver presents. The receiver MUST NOT drop later frames to absorb the loss. It derives no timing for the frames it replaces ( Section 5.1).

The concealment method is an implementation choice: for example holding or replaying the last presented frame, or presenting decoder output in which missing reference data is filled (commonly visible as a solid or green fill). The receiver MUST NOT submit to the decoder a sample that the packaging's reassembly rules have invalidated ( Section 5.2).
The next RAP ends concealment, and the receiver resumes normal decoding from it.

section.name: Audio Blocks
section.t: In-band FEC applies to the blocks of an audio track as to every block, and a receiver MAY request unicast repair for an audio block on the same best-effort terms as for a non-keyframe video block (Section 11.4.5). RAP_flag on an audio packet does not make its block keyframe-bearing; that class applies to video tracks only.

When an audio block is unrecovered, the receiver MUST conceal the lost audio, for example with silence or packet-loss concealment, from the end of the last audio it presented to the authored presentation time of the next audio it presents, and MUST keep the audio clock advancing through the loss. It MUST NOT stall audio presentation waiting for a repair that has not completed by the presentation time of the lost audio.

section.name: Unicast Repair Budget and Priority
section.t: A receiver's unicast repair budget is derived from the catalog, not from a receiver-local rate or byte constant. It is kept per MoQ session and counted in bytes of repair symbol data, a repair symbol of a track counting as that track's symbolSize T (Section 5.1).

li.t: Each block that Section 11.4.1 treats as keyframe-bearing, including a block of unknown class, credits the budget with P_t x T bytes when it reaches its FEC deadline, where P_t is the total repair count of its base instance (Section 6.4.1) and T is its track's symbolSize.
A credit expires when the next keyframe-bearing block of the same source track reaches its FEC deadline, so unspent budget never accumulates beyond one block's credit per source track.
Every unicast repair FETCH debits the budget with the repair symbol bytes it requests.

A keyframe-bearing block's repair is always within budget: the receiver requests at most one repair-track group per base repair layer for it, that is at most the P_t x T bytes that the block itself credits. A receiver MUST NOT have more than one repair FETCH outstanding for the same block and repair layer.

Non-keyframe and audio repair MAY spend only unexpired credit that keyframe-bearing blocks left unspent, and a receiver MUST NOT issue a non-keyframe or audio repair FETCH that the remaining credit does not cover.

A receiver MUST NOT issue a non-keyframe or audio repair FETCH while a keyframe repair FETCH is outstanding on the same session, and SHOULD cancel its outstanding non-keyframe and audio repair FETCHes when a keyframe-bearing block reaches its FEC deadline unrecovered.

section.t: Priorities follow the ranges of Section 10. A keyframe repair FETCH MUST carry a subscriber priority in the Source Media range, numerically at most 191, and numerically no greater than the priority of the source track it repairs where the receiver knows that priority, so that it is delivered ahead of every repair track and is not shed with repair data under congestion. A non-keyframe or audio repair FETCH MUST carry a priority numerically no lower than that of the repair track it fetches, and so at least 192, so that it is shed first.

section.name: Relationship to the Keyframe Overlay
section.t: The keyframe overlay of Section 6.4 and this policy are complementary. The overlay is publisher-side and proactive: it protects RAP fragments across a block of its own, needs no return path, and so also serves sessionless receivers. This policy is receiver-side and reactive: it spends unicast repair only on keyframe-bearing blocks that in-band FEC actually failed to recover, and it needs a MoQ session. A receiver that holds both:

li.t: classifies blocks by Section 11.4.1 whether or not it holds the overlay;
ends its wait for a RAP with whichever of base decoding, overlay decoding, or unicast repair supplies the RAP's fragments first; and

having recovered a block's RAP MFU fragments through the overlay, and holding the FT=0 and FT=1 data units that govern them, conceals the rest of that block's loss as for a non-keyframe block (Section 11.4.3) and SHOULD cancel any outstanding keyframe repair FETCH for it. The overlay covers only packets that set RAP_flag (Section 6.4.2), so it does not by itself recover a lost FT=0 or FT=1 data unit.

section.name: ATSC 3.0 Compatibility
section.t: This specification is designed for interoperability with ATSC A/331 Application-Layer FEC.

section.name: Mapping to A/331 AL-FEC
section.t: overhead is not carried in the catalog; it is converted to and from repairSymbols by the informative rules of Sections 12.2 and 12.3.

Publishers ingesting ATSC 3.0 broadcasts SHOULD preserve the original FEC parameters and pass them through in the catalog fec field. overhead in particular is not passed through verbatim: the catalog carries P rather than a percentage, and overhead is converted as above.

section.name: Sub-Blocks in Broadcast Systems
section.t: This subsection is informative broadcast-interoperability guidance, not an interoperability requirement of this document. Sub-block operation (Section 7.3) remains available to broadcast systems that carry an explicit OTI, such as the A/331 S-TSID fecOTI; the ISO 23008-1 AL-FEC message carries no OTI, and the split source blocks of are the two-stage FEC coding structure of Clause C.2.2, which this document does not use. The number of source symbols per sub-block (K_sub <= K) is derived from the signaled parameters: K_sub = ceil(K / N), where K is the source symbol count (catalog sourceSymbols) and N is the Number of Sub-Blocks field of the explicitly signaled OTI.
When sub-blocks are used:

li.t: interleaveDepthMs keeps its Section 5.1 meaning, the span of the FULL block. A sub-block's own span can be estimated as interleaveDepthMs * K_sub / K for partial-recovery scheduling; the estimate never replaces the full-block field or deadline (Section 9). This enables faster partial recovery at the cost of higher repair overhead (P repair symbols per sub-block instead of per block).
The receiver tracks source symbol arrivals per sub-block (keyed by SBN + sub-block index) and can emit recovered data as soon as each sub-block completes, without waiting for the full block.
The receiver uses the derived sub-block length K_sub (not K from the catalog) for per-sub-block recovery when K_sub < K.

section.t: Sub-blocks are primarily useful for large-K configurations (K >= 64) where full-block recovery latency exceeds acceptable limits.

section.name: Interaction with CMAF Packaging
section.t: This section is informative.
This specification's signaling (Section 5) is container-agnostic, and a repair track can sit alongside a CMAF-packaged source track in the same namespace:

The symbol construction, however, is not container-agnostic: the only source-symbol construction this document specifies is the MMTP-packet construction of Section 7.3. Applying FEC directly to CMAF chunk payloads () would require a companion specification defining the chunk-to-symbol segmentation, padding, length framing, and ESI mapping; none is defined here, and this section sketches the intended track relationship only. A CMAF deployment wanting FEC protection carries the media as mmtp-packaged tracks (an MPU corresponds to a CMAF Fragment; see ).

A segment duration equal to interleaveDepthMs would align each segment boundary with a FEC block boundary, so that a segment holds exactly one block's worth of source symbols and a CDN relay could perform FEC recovery at the segment level before forwarding to FEC-unaware HLS/DASH clients.

section.name: FEC Does Not Provide Confidentiality
section.t: FEC repair symbols are derived from source data. If source data is encrypted, repair symbols will also be encrypted by virtue of operating on ciphertext. However, FEC itself provides no confidentiality guarantees.

section.name: Repair Symbol Manipulation
section.t: An attacker who can modify repair symbols could cause receivers to reconstruct incorrect source data. Integrity protection of repair tracks is RECOMMENDED, using the same mechanisms as source tracks (e.g., QUIC packet protection).

section.name: Amplification
section.t: FEC repair symbols represent additional bandwidth. Publishers MUST NOT generate excessive repair symbols that could be used for bandwidth amplification attacks. The repair overhead (P/K) SHOULD be limited to reasonable values (e.g., <= 50%). The bound applies per FEC instance (Section 6.4.1).

Layering changes the shape of the amplification exposure, because the attacker's lever is now which layers a victim can be made to receive rather than only whether it receives repair at all. Each layer i adds P_i x T bytes per source block, so a receiver induced to hold more layers receives proportionally more repair traffic. Deployments SHOULD bound the number of layers any single receiver may hold, and SHOULD apply the same join authorization to repair-layer endpoints as to media endpoints; a repair-only endpoint (Section 6.3.6) is not less sensitive than a media one merely because it carries no media.

A receiver MUST NOT be made to receive a repair layer it did not join. A publisher or relay MUST NOT push a repair-layer endpoint to a receiver that has not joined it, and MUST NOT add a layer to an endpoint a receiver has already joined as a way of raising that receiver's protection.

section.name: Multicast FEC Security
section.t: When FEC is used over multicast (SSM/AMT), additional considerations apply:

li.t: No QUIC Protection: Multicast UDP lacks QUIC's integrity guarantees. Publishers SHOULD use DTLS-SRTP or equivalent for payload encryption when confidentiality is required.

Repair Injection: Attackers could inject malicious repair symbols on multicast networks. Receivers SHOULD verify FEC block consistency by checking that decoded data matches expected patterns (e.g., valid media container structure).
Source Authentication: See Section 7.1.

Block Integrity: Receivers MAY implement block-level checksums to detect corrupted recovery. If decoded source data fails integrity checks, receivers SHOULD request retransmission via unicast fallback.

Repair Policy Inputs: The in-band evidence that Section 11.4.1 classifies blocks from, and the SSB_length by which Section 7.4 completes a short block, are unauthenticated on bare multicast. An injected packet that marks a block keyframe-bearing costs at most the unicast repair that block's own credit covers (Section 11.4.5). An injected source packet inside a block's gap can instead narrow the bounds of Section 11.4.1 until a keyframe-bearing block is classified otherwise, and an injected repair packet carrying a false SSB_length, accepted before the genuine ones, can mark a block complete early or cause its genuine repair packets to be discarded as inconsistent. Deployments exposed to injection SHOULD authenticate source and repair packets ( Section 7.2).

section.name: ATSC 3.0 Signed Region (A3SA) Considerations
section.t: The Source FEC Payload ID falls outside the A3SA signed region, and neither nor provides a carriage of the SS_ID inside it (Section 8.5). An attacker who can modify it without detection could redirect source symbols to incorrect FEC blocks, causing recovery failures or corrupted output. A receiver that requires authenticated FEC block assignment therefore treats the trailer as Section 8.5 requires. On multicast networks without A3SA verification, receivers SHOULD cross-check the SS_ID against the MMTP packet_sequence_number to detect obvious tampering (e.g., SS_ID values that imply impossible block assignments given the known K and interleave depth).

section.name: No Control Message or Extension Header Registrations
section.t: This document requests no registrations in any MoQ message type or extension header registry. FEC signaling uses no MoQ control message (Section 5.2); no document in this suite requests a control-message codepoint.

section.name: Catalog-Driven FEC
section.t: The subscriber learns the complete FEC configuration from the track's catalog entry before subscribing:

In this flow the track uses 1-second CMAF segments (one MoQ Group per segment), so, as in Appendix B, the 1000 ms interleave window derives D = 1: each Group is one FEC block carrying all K = 32 source objects, followed by P = 8 repair objects. The subscriber's decoder configuration is derived entirely from the catalog fields (Section 4.2): Transfer Length F = K x T = 32 x 1312 = 41,984 bytes, Symbol Size T = 1312, Z = 1, N = 1, Al = 8. No in-session message is required, and this CMAF track carries none.

section.name: Catalog Example
section.t: Complete catalog with FEC and multicast configuration:

Parameter consistency: both tracks use 1-second CMAF segments (one MoQ Group per segment), so the 1000 ms interleave window derives D = round(1000 / 1000) = 1 -- one FEC block per segment -- and K is trivially a multiple of D:

ul.li: Video: 5,000,000 bit/s x 1.0 s / 8 = 625,000 bytes of source data per block; block capacity K x T = 625 x 1000 = 625,000 bytes (exact). Repair overhead P / K = 125 / 625 = 20%.
Audio: 128,000 bit/s x 1.0 s / 8 = 16,000 bytes of source data per block; block capacity K x T = 32 x 512 = 16,384 bytes >= 16,000. Repair overhead P / K = 8 / 32 = 25%.

section.t: The catalog envelope is the MSF root ( Section 5.1); track entries carry the flat base track fields of Section 5.2 (codec, width, samplerate, ...) alongside the fec object this document defines, and inherit the namespace of the catalog track ( Section 5.2.2). The multicast field uses the multicast endpoint format defined in Section 4.1: a one-element endpoints array. Per Section 5, all multicast delivery uses MMTP packets regardless of a track's unicast packaging, so each track listed on the endpoint carries a packetId that routes its MMTP packets on the multicast UDP path.
